rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qārūn attributes his wealth to his own planning and acumen, denies any link to God, and therefore feels no obligation or fear and dismisses the advice he receives.
rows.anchor: he did not owe Him an obligation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God comments that Qarun should have remembered that many earlier peoples stronger than him had been destroyed; Pharaoh's recent drowning was a warning he should have heard about.
rows.anchor: but God had destroyed them in the blink of an eye.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Strength here includes means and resources, majesty and grandeur, and weapons and instruments.
rows.anchor: the might of people viz a viz means and resources, majesty and grandeur, weapons and instruments

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word jamʿ refers to the number of people in a family or tribe.
rows.anchor: refers to the number of people in a family or tribe.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When God seizes criminals, they receive no respite for questioning about their crime or possible pretext; punishment comes immediately.
rows.anchor: they are not given even this much respite that they be asked about their crime and about any pretext they may be having.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Judgement God will not need to investigate wrongdoers because their limbs will testify against them, as also described in Sūrah al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: The forehead, hands, feet and his other limbs will bear wit ness against him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qārūn stages a splendid procession to display his power, overawe Moses and his companions, and increase his own authority; such displays impress ordinary people and are used by social leaders.
rows.anchor: impresses the common man the most.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who regard worldly wealth as everything react to Qārūn's display by calling him fortunate.
rows.anchor: they cried out that Q ārūn was a very lucky person.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The knowledgeable urge people to seek faith, righteous deeds, and their reward rather than a display of wealth; only the steadfast can hold to this wisdom against worldly lures.
rows.anchor: faith and righteous deeds and their reward.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Real knowledge is awareness of God and the Hereafter, which gives people true illumination; technical competence alone is not this knowledge.
rows.anchor: real knowledge or the knowledge of God’s comprehension and of the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without real knowledge, even expertise can serve greed or produce cleverness without humanity; such cunning is dangerous, like a sword in a naïve person's hands, and Satan exemplifies guile.
rows.anchor: such cleverness and craftiness is very dangerous.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in the statement about receiving wisdom refers back to the wisdom and sagacity urged by the knowledgeable, an antecedent that can occur this way in Arabic.
rows.anchor: is the wisdom and sagacity which these people of knowledge urged them to adopt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Real knowledge and patience go together: true wisdom belongs to those able to sacrifice even their greatest assets for the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: real knowledge and patience are pairs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage asks whether the patience clause is spoken by the men of learning or inserted by God as praise for them.
rows.anchor: is it an insertion by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account suppresses that, after the Samiri episode, Moses challenged Qārūn and his companions to a mutual imprecation by the worship tent; Numbers 16:27–34 describes the earth swallowing the challengers and their households.
rows.anchor: invited Q ārūn and his companions to a mub āhalah (cursing and ill-praying) in front of the worship tent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qārūn and his companions were swallowed by the earth following Moses' prayer, leaving Qārūn unable to defend himself and his people unable to rescue him.
rows.anchor: Q ārūn and his companions were submerged in the earth as a result of the curse and prayer of Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After witnessing Qārūn's fate, those who had envied his position thank God for sparing them and recognize that God gives provision abundantly or sparingly as He wills; disbelievers do not succeed.
rows.anchor: When they witnessed his fate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In classical Arabic, ams can mean the recent past as well as yesterday, so the speakers were recently infatuated with Qārūn's splendour.
rows.anchor: It also refers to the recent past.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wayl is an Arabic word of admonition, comparable to the English expression goodness me; with the added particles, it conveys that reaction to what follows.
rows.anchor: is a word of admonition.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase meaning for whom He wills is omitted after the statement that God gives provision, by parallelism; the translation supplies the suppressed words.
rows.anchor: The translation reveals this suppression.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qarun anecdote also subtly depicts the character and fate of Abu Lahab and his followers: their trial mirrors the trial of Moses' community through Qarun.
rows.anchor: this anecdote of Q ārūn was not cited as a past happening.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qārūn was the richest Levite and Moses' cousin; Abu Lahab was the wealthiest Hashimite and Muhammad's paternal uncle, giving them parallel tribal and family positions.
rows.anchor: the most affluent person of the Hashimites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both were major capitalists; Abu Lahab controlled the House of God's keys and treasury, accumulating great wealth by fair means or foul, later referenced in Sūrahs al-Humazah and al-Lahab.
rows.anchor: Ab ū Lahab held the keys of the House of God and was the sole custodian of the treasury of the House of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both men were miserly, arrogant, and hard-hearted.
rows.anchor: Both were very stingy, arrogant and hard-hearted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both bore malice toward their messengers: Qārūn sought tribal religious leadership to protect his capitalist plans, while Abu Lahab wanted to retain control of the House's keys and public treasury.
rows.anchor: same malice for their respective messenger s.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their fates likewise resemble one another: both incurred God's wrath, and Abu Lahab's fate will be described in Sūrah al-Lahab.
rows.anchor: Both were seized by God’s wrath.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qarun account presents Abu Lahab and his die-hard followers in Qarun's guise; recognizing this allusion is necessary to understand the story's wisdom.
rows.anchor: the character of Ab ū Lahab and his die-hard followers that is actually mentioned in the garb of Q ārūn.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hereafter's abode is reserved for those free of arrogance and earthly disorder, who live as God's servants and advocate His just social order; they are the truly pious and ultimately successful.
rows.anchor: system of justice and fairness prescribed by God in the society they live in.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here najʿaluhā means to reserve something especially for someone or something.
rows.anchor: to reserve someone especially for something

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God deals graciously with those who bring good deeds, rewarding them beyond their deserts, and justly gives wrongdoers the exact recompense of what they did.
rows.anchor: He will reward them much more than they deserve.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah's closing verses assure the Prophet that God will help him fulfill his Qur'an responsibility and reach a good end; he should persist in propagation despite opponents, with God supporting him.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) has been assured that he has not asked the Almighty to reveal the Qur’ ān to him that he should fret over it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maʿād means culmination, fate, or place of return.
rows.anchor: means “culmination, fate and place of return.”
